session_title: First 'Pet Partners' Experience Day Event Held

content.text: Ms. Zhou, today's Pet Partner Experience Day has come to a successful conclusion! I'm sending you a photo from the event—the atmosphere was incredibly warm and harmonious. It has been exactly five months since we first discussed this plan back in July, and now it has finally transformed from an idea into reality.

Director Lin, the event was so well organized! For the children, such an experience is truly invaluable. I observed that the kids were a bit nervous at first, but An An is great with children and quickly helped them relax. It reminded me of when I shared photos of my daughters with An An on the lawn in May, and your son looked so envious. Now, he finally has the chance to experience it too.

Yes, our community has such activities, and everyone is very happy. My little one is especially excited and keeps asking when we can come again next time. The other participating families have also responded very positively. Families with pets feel they have gained helpers and playmates, while families without pets have fulfilled their children's wishes. As mentioned during our annual review, the Pet Companion Program already has three families signed up for the trial run, and today marks its official launch.

What matters is that I saw the Golden Retriever patiently following the child's slow pace, and a little girl grooming a cat under her parent's guidance—all interactions were safe and orderly. Perhaps we should consider making such temporary activities regular and standardized, just like the rotating health assistant system we discussed earlier, to establish a sustainable mechanism.

Let's discuss this together! I think we can establish a fixed pairing list and activity schedule, similar to what we did with the rotation for the health assistant. Remember during our discussion in July, I created an activity rules table. Now would be a good time to refine it to ensure that every activity has parental accompaniment and supervision.

For children, regular activities can foster a sense of responsibility. I suggest we refer to the priority projects mentioned during the annual review and prioritize the Pet Companion Program for 2025. As confirmed during our review on December 25th, the Health Corner and the Pet Companion Program can be prioritized for implementation. Now that the Health Assistant linkage has been launched, the Pet Companion Program should follow suit.

Ms. Zhou, look at this photo. It was taken near the end of the event. Someone was playing the guitar, and the dog was quietly listening nearby. The atmosphere was particularly heartwarming. This reminds me that we could introduce some simple pet behavior training, such as how to properly use a leash to ensure safety. Just as you mentioned when sharing your pet-raising experience in May, training requires patience and rules.

This is a great idea! The important thing is that training can help children learn to respect animals. We can start with the basics, such as teaching them proper feeding and leash-handling methods, just like we emphasized a step-by-step approach when discussing food education sharing. Remember when we talked about parent-child kitchens in August, we said 'start with small things'—the same applies to pet training.

Our community has resources, and I can reach out to some pet trainers to offer public welfare lectures. At the same time, we can create an activity rule sheet, similar to the safety responsibility agreement for shared kitchens, to ensure that parents accompany and supervise each event. Just like when we discussed the neighborhood potluck in September, we emphasized food safety and task allocation.

You could try this approach: as one of the first families to participate, I can help gather feedback. For children, regular group activities can enhance their sense of community belonging, much like the resident co-creation emphasized during the cultural festival planning. Looking back at our historical conversations, we’ve progressed from health support to emotional education for pets, and now we’re deepening these efforts into regular activities. Each step is built on the foundation of trust established earlier.

Ms. Zhou, I found a tutorial diagram on dog leash training and am sending it to you. We can use this as a basis to design simple training content, allowing children to learn while having fun. This reminds me of the textbook selection suggestion table you shared earlier—systematic guidance is very helpful for children.

This picture is very practical! The key is to make training fun and avoid monotony. We can incorporate elements of nature exploration from the parent-child activity idea bank, such as setting up a small obstacle course in the community for children to practice leash skills. Just like the nature treasure hunt and cardboard castle we discussed in early December when talking about low-cost parent-child activities, we can integrate education into play.

Everyone pitching in will keep the costs low. We can use old materials, like items recycled from flea markets, to make training props. This approach is not only environmentally friendly but also gets the kids involved. Back in November, when we discussed the Old Things, New Life project, we emphasized the educational value of resource recycling.

For children, the process of hands-on creation itself is a great learning experience. I suggest we could organize a regular event each month, such as on the afternoon of the third weekend, with the schedule announced in advance to help families plan accordingly. Just like the duty roster for a health assistant, regular activities can help cultivate children's habit of consistent participation.

Great idea! Our community can take charge of venue coordination and promotion, just like organizing the Health Corner event. Teacher Zhou, as an education expert, could you help design some feedback forms to collect opinions after the event? Similar to the feedback forms you created for the Health Steward program, timely follow-up is crucial.

Of course! It's important to follow up promptly to ensure the event is continuously optimized. I can refer to the feedback mechanism from the previous Health Assistant event and create a simple questionnaire so that both children and parents can easily participate. Looking back at past conversations, I always enjoy following up on feedback, and I'll continue that habit this time as well.

Great! This means the Pet Companion Program can transition from a pilot phase to a regular initiative. We can also expand it further, such as by inviting elderly individuals living alone to participate, as previously mentioned, to enhance intergenerational connections. We had already considered extending the program to elderly individuals living alone during our discussions in July, and now we can gradually make it happen.

For children, this can cultivate their empathy and sense of social responsibility. We can proceed step by step, first consolidating basic activities, then evaluating and expanding, just like testing the waters with the Mid-Autumn family banquet as envisioned in the shared kitchen concept. From an annual review perspective, the neighborhood family banquet is still in the discussion stage, while the pet companion initiative can take the lead.

Dear Teacher Zhou, thank you for your support! This event has successfully tested the waters and received positive feedback, laying the foundation for its regular operation next year. Let's work together to make the Pet Partner Program a highlight of community connection. Just as we discussed when planning the cultural festival on December 20th, we aim to evolve from neighborhood mutual assistance to collaborative co-construction.

Director Lin, it's been a pleasure working with you! What matters most is that through each event, we have deepened our relationship from neighborhood mutual assistance to trust and sharing. I look forward to more exciting moments next year and working together to elevate the collaboration between home, school, and community to new heights. Starting from helping each other when the child fell ill in March to now with the pet companion project taking shape, our bond has grown stronger and deeper.
